Question Choices: Select all that apply. Statistics involves: ~~Collecting-data | Presenting-data | Analyzing-data~~
Hints: Look for a collection of observations whose values may vary; yes/no responses also count as data.
Solution: Statistics includes collecting data, presenting or organizing it, and analyzing patterns and variability. Select all three choices.

Question Choices: Select. Asked once of one person, is this a statistical question? "Do you like soccer?" ~~Yes | No~~
Hints: Look for a collection of observations whose values may vary; yes/no responses also count as data.
Solution: Asked once of one person, this requests one response rather than a distribution of varying responses: No. Yes/no answers ARE data, and asking the same question of many people can form a statistical investigation.

Question Choices: Which is statistical? A. "What is tomorrow's bus fare?"  B. "How much do students spend on lunch each day this month?"
Hints: Look for a collection of observations whose values may vary; yes/no responses also count as data.
Solution: This asks about measurements across students or across multiple days. It anticipates variation in those observations and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data, so it is statistical.

Question Choices: Two classes recorded reading time (in hours): Class A: 2, 2.1, 2, 2.2, 2.1  Class B: 1, 3.5, 2, 4, 0.5. Which class has more variability? Answer A or B
Hints: Compare maximum minus minimum for each data set.
Solution: Range A=2.2−2=0.2; range B=4−0.5=3.5. B has the greater range and more variability by this measure.

Question Choices: Select all changes that ask for data whose values may vary. Original question: "How many minutes did I exercise today?": ~~How-many-minutes-did-I-exercise-today-and-yesterday? | How-many-minutes-do-students-in-my-class-exercise-each-day? | Did-I-exercise-today?~~
Hints: Look for a collection of observations whose values may vary; yes/no responses also count as data.
Solution: Select the first and second choices. Sleep or exercise time can vary across two nights/days for one person, as well as across many students. A single yes/no response about one day does not ask for a distribution. Statistical questions anticipate variability; they do not require different people.
